content: Morphea, also referred to as localized scleroderma, is a condition characterized by the thickening and hardening of the skin and underlying subcutaneous tissues due to excessive collagen deposition. This condition encompasses a spectrum of presentations, ranging from small, localized plaques confined to the skin to more extensive disease that can result in significant functional and cosmetic deformities. Unlike systemic sclerosis, morphea is generally limited to the skin and does not typically involve internal organs. Morphea is classified into five main subtypes: plaque morphea, generalized morphea, linear scleroderma, bullous morphea, and deep morphea. However, this classification does not account for a mixed form of morphea, where multiple types of skin lesions coexist in the same individual. It is estimated that up to 15% of patients with morphea may fall into this mixed category, which has only recently been recognized. Morphea is considered an uncommon condition, with an estimated prevalence of 1 in 100,000 individuals. However, the true incidence and prevalence remain unclear due to a lack of comprehensive studies. Additionally, morphea may be underdiagnosed, as smaller plaques may not prompt referral to specialists, and some physicians may be unfamiliar with the condition. Similar to other connective tissue and autoimmune disorders, morphea predominantly affects women, with a female-to-male ratio of approximately 3:1. The exact cause of morphea remains unknown. Observational studies and case reports suggest a potential link to autoimmune processes, as patients with morphea often have a family history of autoimmune diseases. Laboratory tests have identified higher frequencies of certain autoantibodies, such as anti-histone and anti-topoisomerase IIa antibodies, in individuals with morphea. Additionally, morphea has been reported to coexist with other systemic autoimmune diseases, including primary biliary cirrhosis, vitiligo, and systemic lupus erythematosus, further supporting its classification as an autoimmune condition. When diagnosing morphea, it is important to differentiate it from other conditions that may present with similar clinical features.g., bleomycin, silicone implants, or pesticides). Physical examination of patients with morphea typically reveals localized areas of skin thickening and hardening. These lesions may vary in size, shape, and depth, depending on the subtype of morphea. In some cases, nodular or plaque-like lesions may be observed on the trunk or other areas of the body. Over the years, various treatment approaches have been explored for morphea, including topical, intralesional, and systemic corticosteroids. Antimalarial drugs such as hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine have also been utilized. Other immunomodulatory agents, including methotrexate, topical tacrolimus, and penicillamine, have been tried with varying degrees of success. Phototherapy, particularly ultraviolet A (UVA) light, has been employed as well.
